text:
There are active civil cases involving RICO allegations and securities-law claims tied to Vivek Ramaswamy

Civil RICO-related case (GloriFi)
A federal civil racketeering lawsuit was filed in May 2024 in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Georgia by parties connected to the failed “anti-woke” financial startup GloriFi (including founder Toby Neugebauer). It named Ramaswamy among defendants (along with figures such as Peter Thiel). 

The complaint alleged violations of the federal civil RICO statute and Georgia racketeering law, plus related claims of trade-secret theft, conspiracy, and misappropriation of confidential information/ideas. It claimed Ramaswamy was offered a significant stake and CEO role in a planned GloriFi anti-ESG asset-management venture (described as “WhiteRock”) in late 2021, then launched Strive Asset Management months later with a similar mission and early energy-fund focus.

Status: The Georgia case was stayed and administratively closed in 2024 pending GloriFi’s Chapter 7 bankruptcy in Texas. In June 2025, a bankruptcy judge ruled that most of the RICO and related claims described injuries to GloriFi itself (making them property of the bankruptcy estate rather than personal claims), enjoined the existing litigation in its then-current form, and noted plaintiffs could seek authority to pursue non-derivative claims. No court has ruled on the merits or found Ramaswamy liable. Broader GloriFi bankruptcy litigation continues into 2026, and Ramaswamy remains entangled as an investor and named party in the related disputes. Reports describe aspects of the case as still proceeding in the federal system.

Securities-related whistleblower lawsuit (Strive / Rosely)
Former Strive Asset Management executive Joyce Rosely sued Strive, co-founder Anson Frericks, and Ramaswamy (case 2:23-cv-20772, District of New Jersey). She alleged that “almost immediately” after starting in August 2022, Ramaswamy and Frericks pressured her and others to violate securities laws. Cited examples included using noncompliant sales materials that improperly promised future returns, having employees engage in sales before licenses transferred, distributing unapproved materials, involving unregistered employees in client discussions, soliciting for products before they were registered/trading, and unlicensed sales activity (including alleged activity by Ramaswamy on Twitter). She claimed she and another employee objected and were later fired in retaliation (March 2023).

Status: On August 25, 2026, U.S. District Judge Julien Xavier Neals denied the motion to dismiss the core whistleblower retaliation claims against Ramaswamy personally (under New Jersey’s Conscientious Employee Protection Act). The judge found the complaint sufficiently alleged supervisory authority, demands to violate securities laws, receipt of objections, and participation in the firing decision. Those claims (and the related claim against the company) remain active and are proceeding. Some other claims (e.g., certain discrimination allegations) were dismissed without prejudice. The court has not determined whether any securities-law violations actually occurred. Ramaswamy and Strive have denied the allegations, describing the termination as part of a reorganization.

Wikipedia’s entry on Ramaswamy notes the August 2026 ruling allowing the whistleblower claims to proceed without a finding on the underlying securities allegations. A similar overlapping suit by another former employee (John Phillips) was also filed earlier.

I SENT MY PASTOR A PHOTO MEANT FOR MY BOYFRIEND

I was getting ready and took a picture for my boyfriend. Just me in the bathroom mirror, nothing on. I typed his name and hit send without looking twice. A second later my stomach dropped. It had gone to Pastor Daniels instead.
I stared at the screen. He opened it right away. The three dots appeared, then disappeared, then appeared again. Finally he replied: “We should talk about this.”

I typed back fast, trying to explain it was a mistake meant for my boyfriend. He said he understood, but the messages kept coming. Little things at first. He started staying after service to talk to me. Then he began texting in the evenings, asking how I was, saying he had been thinking about me. When I tried to keep it short he would call. His voice was calm, but the things he said were not. He told me the picture was still on his phone. He told me he had not been able to stop looking at it.

I kept saying no. I told him I had a boyfriend. I told him it was wrong. He did not push hard, just stayed close. He offered to come by the house for the usual visit, the one he did with a few families. I said yes because I did not know how to say no without making it worse.

He arrived in the afternoon. We sat in the living room. He asked about my boyfriend. I answered. Then he moved closer on the couch. He put his hand on my knee and said he had been patient. I felt my chest get tight. I told him he should leave. He said he would if I really wanted him to. I did not answer.

We stayed like that for a long time. When he finally stood up to go, he asked if he could come back tomorrow. I nodded. After he left I sat there and knew I would not stop him next time. I already knew how it would go once he did.

text:
Tucked within the historic Trikuteshwara Temple complex is a building that could easily be overshadowed by its larger neighbour. But step into the Saraswati Temple and the scale of its artistic ambition becomes immediately apparent.
Dating to around the mid-11th century, this Western Chalukyan shrine contains some of the most extraordinary stone carving I have encountered in Karnataka. Its open mandapa is supported by pillars of astonishing variety: some covered with miniature shrines, gods and celestial figures barely a few centimetres high; others shaped into star-like profiles or decorated with deeply cut geometric lattices.

Why so many different designs in one relatively small space? Was every pillar part of a carefully conceived architectural scheme, or were individual craftsmen allowed to experiment and display their own skills? I rather like the possibility that this was a place of artistic invention as much as devotion.

The sculptured parapet walls deserve just as much attention. Circular medallions filled with animated figures sit above rows of delicate standing figures and auspicious vessels, all framed by intricate foliate scrollwork.
Overhead, the surviving vaulted ceiling has intersecting stone ribs and pendant lotus buds, almost as though a timber roof had been translated into stone.

Inside the sanctum sits Saraswati, goddess of learning, music and the arts. Already badly mutilated when first documented, the sculpture suffered further vandalism in July 2026 - a deeply troubling reminder of the fragility of this irreplaceable heritage.
Saraswati may be modest in size, but few temples of comparable scale offer such an extraordinary concentration of craftsmanship.
#SaraswatiTemple

In 1950, the first US nuclear weapon entered Canadian soil when the US Air Force Strategic Air Command (SAC) stationed 11 model 1561 Fat Man atomic bombs at RCAF Station Goose Bay in Labrador. Goose Bay was used as an aircraft staging location for both the SAC and the Royal Air Force's V Force. The bombs were landed; crews relieved; aircraft refueled, or repaired; without returning to bases in the continental US. Nuclear weapons designs of the time were easily damaged but precise devices, that required off-aircraft inspection (after landing), and environmental sheltering (at a secure warm/dry location) while their carrier aircraft was on the ground for routine maintenance or repair.[2]

From 1963 to 1984, the US deployed a total of four tactical nuclear weapons systems in Canada, which amounted to several hundred nuclear warheads.[3]

Throughout the Cold War, Canada was closely aligned with defensive elements of United States programs in both NORAD and NATO. The ratlines (German: Rattenlinien) were systems of escape routes used by Nazis and their collaborators to flee Europe from 1945 onwards in the aftermath of World War II. Two primary routes developed independently with their operators eventually collaborating, the first transferring through Spain and the second through Rome and Genoa. Some escapees settled at these locations or used them to flee elsewhere, with the majority settling in Argentina or other South American countries such as Brazil, Chile, and Paraguay.

The ratlines were supported by some clergy of the Catholic Church, such as Austrian bishop Alois Hudal and Croatian priest Krunoslav Draganović, as well as some outlets of the International Committee of the Red Cross. The Nazis paid Argentine officials (starting c. 1943) to shield their agents, bolstering the rise of Juan Perón, whose regime set up additional ratlines through Scandinavia and Switzerland.

A number of significant Nazis and their collaborators escaped, including Ustaše leader Ante Pavelić, as well as Schutzstaffel (SS) officers Adolf Eichmann and Josef Mengele, both perpetrators of the Holocaust. Starting in 1945, the United States utilized the ratlines to aid the escape of some Soviet defectors and informants, as well as Gestapo leader Klaus Barbie (who had traded intel with the U.S. Army while being held in Austria). Decades later, the ratlines remain a subject of investigation[b] and cultural interest.

Operation Paperclip was a secret United States intelligence program in which more than 1,600 German scientists, engineers, and technicians were taken from former Nazi Germany to the US between 1945 and 1959 for government employment after the end of World War II in Europe; several were confirmed to be former members of the Nazi Party, including the SS or the SA.

The effort began in earnest in 1945, as the Allies advanced into Germany and discovered a wealth of scientific talent and advanced research that had contributed to Germany's wartime technological advancements. The US Joint Chiefs of Staff officially established Operation Overcast (operations "Overcast" and "Paperclip" were related, and the terms are often used interchangeably) on July 20, 1945, with the dual aims of leveraging German expertise for the ongoing war effort against Japan and to bolster US postwar military research. The operation, conducted by the Joint Intelligence Objectives Agency (JIOA), was largely actioned by special agents of the US Army's Counterintelligence Corps (CIC). Many selected scientists were involved in the Nazi rocket program, aviation, or chemical/biological warfare. The Soviet Union in the following year conducted a similar program, called Operation Osoaviakhim, that emphasized many of the same fields of research.

The operation, characterized by the recruitment of German specialists and their families, relocated more than 1500 experts to the US. It has been valued at US$10 billion in patents and industrial processes. Recruits included such notable figures as Wernher von Braun, a leading rocket-technology scientist. Those recruited were instrumental in the development of the US space program and military technology during the Cold War. Despite its contributions to American scientific advances, Operation Paperclip has been controversial because of the Nazi affiliations of many recruits, and the ethics of assimilating individuals associated with war crimes into American society.

The operation was not solely focused on rocketry; it also transferred expertise in aerodynamics, aviation medicine, and related military research. Its technological legacy was especially visible in the transformation of German V-2 rocket technology into later American missile and launch systems. After moving to Redstone Arsenal in 1950, Wernher von Braun’s team developed the Redstone and Jupiter missiles. When this group was transferred to the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) in 1960, it became central to the work of the Marshall Space Flight Center and the development of the Saturn launch vehicles used in the Apollo program. The related Mercury-Redstone rocket also carried Alan Shepard on the first American human spaceflight.[1][2]

In aeronautics, German high-speed flight research and aerodynamic knowledge contributed to postwar American aircraft and missile development. In aviation medicine, German specialists contributed to early space medicine research in the United States, including studies on weightlessness, life-support systems, and human performance in extreme conditions.[3][4]

Operation Paperclip was part of a broader strategy by the US to harness German scientific talent in the face of emerging Cold War tensions, and ensure this expertise did not fall into the hands of the Soviet Union or other nations. The operation's legacy has remained controversial in subsequent decades.

A socialist state, socialist republic, or socialist country is a sovereign state constitutionally dedicated to the establishment of socialism. This article is about states that refer to themselves as socialist states, and not specifically about communist states that refer to themselves as socialist states. It includes information on liberal democratic states with constitutional references to socialism as well as other state formations that have referred to themselves as socialist.

Constitutional references to socialism
A number of countries that make references to socialism in their constitutions are not communist states. In most cases, these are constitutional references to the building of a socialist society and political principles that have little to no bearing on the structure and guidance of these country's machinery of government and economic system. The preamble to the 1976 Constitution of Portugal states that the Portuguese state has, as one of its goals, opening "the way to socialist society".[1] Another broad example is that of Slovenia, which defines itself as a "state governed by the rule of law and a social state".[2] Algeria, the Congo, India, and Sri Lanka have directly used the term socialist in their official constitution and name. Croatia, Hungary, and Poland directly denounce "Communism" in their founding documents in reference to their past regimes.[i]

In these cases, the intended meaning of socialism can vary widely and sometimes the constitutional references to socialism are left over from a previous period in the country's history. In the case of many Middle Eastern states, the term socialism was often used in reference to an Arab socialist/nationalist philosophy adopted by specific regimes, such as that of Gamal Abdel Nasser and that of the various Ba'ath parties. Examples of countries directly using the term socialist in their names include the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka and the Socialist Republic of Vietnam, while a number of countries make references to socialism in their constitutions, but not in their names. These include India[3] and Portugal. In addition, countries such as Belarus, Colombia, France, Russia, and Spain use the varied term social state, leaving a more ambiguous meaning. In the constitutions of Croatia, Hungary, and Poland, direct condemnation is made to the respective past socialist regimes.[4] The autonomous region of Rojava, which operates under the principles of democratic confederalism, has been described as a socialist state.[5]

text:
Wednesday morning headlines from #Azerbaijan, 28 October

● The seventh World Forum for Intercultural Dialogue has opened in Baku, with President Ilham Aliyev addressing the opening session. He said the forum had become a major international platform over the past 15 years, with more than 2,000 participants from over 100 countries attending this year. Aliyev focused on the outcome of the 2020 Second Karabakh War, saying Azerbaijan had restored its territorial integrity and subsequently offered peace to Armenia. He accused the international community of applying double standards, arguing that UN Security Council resolutions recognising Karabakh as part of Azerbaijan had gone unimplemented for 30 years and that Armenia had faced no sanctions as an occupying power. Aliyev also warned of external threats, criticised other countries for trying to dictate terms to Baku and presented Azerbaijan as an independent actor, reliable energy supplier and transport hub.

● Hikmat Hajiyev, an aide to the Azerbaijani president, said at the forum that Armenia and Armenian society should apologise to the Azerbaijani people for depriving hundreds of thousands of Azerbaijanis of the opportunity to return to their homes for decades. He said Azerbaijan was not seeking revenge but considered recognition of historical responsibility necessary for lasting peace.

● Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov held talks on the sidelines of the forum with the head of the UN’s tourism agency, UN Tourism, and the head of the Islamic World Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (ICESCO). They discussed expanding cooperation in tourism, including developing new destinations in territories Azerbaijan regained control of after the 2020 Second Karabakh War. Preserving cultural heritage and restoring cultural and religious monuments were also highlighted as areas for cooperation. The importance of ICESCO’s regional office in Baku was also discussed.

● Azerbaijan, Iran, Kazakhstan, Russia and Turkmenistan must urgently work together to address the Caspian Sea’s falling water levels, Shahin Mustafayev, president of the International Turkic Academy, said at the forum. He warned that the decline threatened biodiversity and the livelihoods of communities across all five coastal countries. He called for the countries to share scientific data and coordinate their policies.

● Ramiz Mehdiyev (pictured below), a former head of the Azerbaijani presidential administration, has been sentenced to 14 years in prison, but the sentence has been suspended because of his age and health. The court also ordered his property confiscated by the state and stripped him of his state awards.

Mehdiyev headed the presidential administration from 1995 to 2019 and was widely regarded as Azerbaijan’s powerful behind-the-scenes political figure. He was found guilty of treason, attempting to seize power by force and money laundering. He has also been reported to face bribery allegations. The criminal case against him was opened in October 2025. Investigators alleged that he had taken part in plans to seize power with the help of foreign intelligence services. The authorities did not identify the services, but Russia was mentioned in case-related materials and local media discussions.

● Nurlan Libre (Gahramanly), a journalist with Meydan TV who is in pre-trial detention, said prison officers took his notes for preparing witness questioning during a search of his cell and then physically assaulted him in the detention centre director’s office. He said he was subsequently placed in a punishment cell for three days. Libre rejected the official explanation that he had obstructed the search, claiming the punishment was linked to his reporting on restrictions on wearing the hijab in Azerbaijani schools. His lawyers said his right to mount a defence had been violated. A court hearing at which witnesses were due to be questioned was postponed.

Twelve journalists are on trial in the Meydan TV case, facing charges including currency smuggling and other offences. All deny wrongdoing and say the case is linked to their critical reporting on the authorities.

● Mirsaleh Seyidov, head of Azerbaijan’s Penitentiary Service and a deputy justice minister, has been dismissed. No official reason has been given. Azerbaijan’s service of Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty reported repeated complaints during his tenure about torture and ill-treatment of prisoners, inadequate access to medical care and poor detention conditions, particularly from political prisoners. The Penitentiary Service rejected the criticism.

● The first Azerbaijan-EU think tank forum has been held in Brussels, jointly organised by Azerbaijan’s Centre of Analysis of International Relations (AIR Center) and Belgium’s Egmont Institute. Discussions covered regional security, energy cooperation and the development of transport routes, including the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) and the Middle Corridor. Speakers highlighted the growing importance of trade routes across the Caspian Sea linking Europe with Central Asia following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

● Bart Ouvry, head of the Egmont Institute, said the EU should develop ties with Azerbaijan through concrete economic projects that could make bilateral relations more sustainable. Addressing tensions between Azerbaijan and some European institutions, particularly the European Parliament, he said continued dialogue could help both sides better understand each other’s positions.

● Farid Shafiyev, head of the AIR Center, said Azerbaijan and the EU needed a new agreement reflecting deeper cooperation in energy, transport and the reconstruction of territories affected by conflict. He also said Armenia’s constitution needed to be amended before a peace treaty could be signed, arguing that it contained territorial claims against Azerbaijan. Shafiyev said Baku and Yerevan could negotiate directly without mediators. He expressed hope that opponents of the peace process, including members of the Armenian diaspora in Europe, would not derail the current opportunity to normalise relations.

● Devlet Bahçeli, leader of Turkey’s Nationalist Movement Party (MHP), said the brotherhood between Azerbaijan and Turkey was rooted in deep historical ties. He added that unity among Turkic peoples should be based on equality and mutual respect.

Context: His remarks come amid tensions between the two countries. In Turkey, there has been sharp criticism of Azerbaijan’s new secular school uniform rules, which effectively ban the hijab in schools. Turkish media and social media users have also criticised Azerbaijan’s cooperation with Israel. Baku has responded with strong statements against what it sees as attempts to interfere in the country’s internal affairs.

● An international symposium titled “From Kars to Nakhchivan: Turkey-Azerbaijan Diplomacy and the Future of the Turkic World” was held in Ankara. Participants included officials, diplomats, academics and journalists from Turkey, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan. Discussions focused on strengthening ties between Turkic states, combating disinformation, media cooperation and developing regional transport routes. Speakers highlighted the role of the partnership between Baku and Ankara in promoting unity across the Turkic world.

● Azerbaijani Energy Minister Parviz Shahbazov held separate meetings in Moscow with Russia’s energy minister and Iran’s acting oil minister. The talks focused on developing bilateral energy cooperation.

● Algeria has invited Azerbaijani oil and gas companies to take part in an international tender for exploration in seven areas of the country. The issue was discussed at a Moscow meeting between Shahbazov and Algeria’s hydrocarbons minister. Particular attention was given to potential cooperation between Azerbaijan’s state oil company SOCAR and Algeria’s Sonatrach, including field development, well services, raw material transport, oil refining and petrochemicals. The first meeting of a joint working group between the two countries is planned for November in Baku.

● Azerbaijan’s Economy Ministry and Spain’s IE University have signed an agreement to establish an Economic Observatory. It will analyse economic trends, examine ways to improve Azerbaijan’s competitiveness and prepare recommendations for the country’s economic policy.

● Baku is hosting the third meeting of heads of law enforcement agencies from member states of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC). More than 250 representatives from 48 countries are taking part. During the meeting, Azerbaijan’s Prosecutor General’s Office signed cooperation memorandums with Morocco and Iraq on exchanging information and methods for preventing and investigating corruption offences.

● Azerbaijan has backed the candidacy of UAE Minister of State Lana Zaki Nusseibeh for the post of UN secretary-general.

● Azerbaijan’s National Cybersecurity Agency has warned of a rise in WhatsApp account hacks. Scammers may gain access to users’ messages through linked devices. The agency advises users to check WhatsApp’s “Linked Devices” section and log out any unfamiliar devices, enable two-step verification, and never share SMS verification codes or their PIN. Users should also avoid suspicious links and fake messages claiming to come from WhatsApp support.

text:
How CoreWeave finances GPUs through ring-fenced contracts

Michael Intrator, Aravind Srinivas, Arthur Mensch and Daniel Roberts on All-In with Jason Calacanis. Michael Intrator says he started CoreWeave in 2017 after running an algorithmic hedge fund, first using GPUs for crypto mining before moving into AI infrastructure. Aravind Srinivas leads Perplexity, which he describes as built around accurate answers and expanded from search into browser and computer products. Arthur Mensch leads Mistral AI, which builds open models and enterprise customization tools. Daniel Roberts co-founded IREN with his brother, initially building data centers for Bitcoin mining and now shifting capacity toward AI.

Intrator says demand for AI compute continues to exceed available capacity and argues that long contracts and ring-fenced financing support CoreWeave's infrastructure investments. Srinivas says Perplexity's edge is orchestration across specialized models, with computer and hybrid local/server execution aimed at automating personal and enterprise work. Mensch argues that open models let companies customize AI on their own infrastructure, while production agents need governance, observability and access controls. Roberts says IREN's early investment in data-center sites and power positions it to shift from Bitcoin mining toward AI compute, though construction and supply constraints set the pace.

Minute by minute

1. CoreWeave's GPU roots became AI infrastructure (0:26)
Intrator says CoreWeave began with an algorithmic natural-gas hedge fund, then used GPUs for crypto mining after deciding Bitcoin ASICs were a poor fit. The company moved into rendering and batch computing, then donated A100s to Eleuther AI to learn neural-network workloads. Researchers later became customers. He says the experience showed that scale and software operations would define the AI infrastructure business.

2. Older GPUs remain commercially useful (10:00)
Intrator rejects claims that GPUs become obsolete in 16 months or two years, noting CoreWeave's average customer contract runs five years and it uses six-year depreciation. He says older A100s remain useful for new companies and less cutting-edge workloads, and their price appreciated during the year. He also says NVIDIA allocates GPUs to customers in the order they place their orders.

3. CoreWeave finances compute through boxes (18:33)
Intrator says CoreWeave puts a customer contract, GPUs and a data-center contract into a financing structure called a box. Its cash flow pays operating costs and debt service before returning any remainder to CoreWeave. He says the structure helped the company raise $35 billion in 18 months. On a five-year deal, principal and interest are paid off within two and a half years, and its cost of capital fell 600 basis points over two years.

4. AI demand strains the full supply chain (23:33)
Intrator says demand has overwhelmed global compute capacity for four years and that long contracts with strong counterparties help protect CoreWeave and its lenders if demand suddenly falls. He names power, memory, storage, networking and optics as constraints, and describes memory fabs as a capital-intensive, cyclical business. Calacanis cites the price of a million tokens falling from $32 and change at ChatGPT's launch to nine cents. Intrator links falling costs to engineering and competition.

5. Accuracy leads Perplexity's product strategy (32:55)
Srinivas says accuracy has been Perplexity's priority. The product began with web-grounded answers, added Comet browser agents and now offers Computer, which coordinates different models and tools. He describes the models as specialized instruments, with Computer responsible for producing the finished task.

6. Personal AI blends local and cloud execution (37:00)
Srinivas says Personal Computer will synchronize Perplexity Computer with a user's local machine, with a Mac mini acting as a local server for private data and server-side compute available for longer tasks with permission. He favors a hybrid setup over an all-local or all-cloud choice. He describes AI as an operating system that starts from objectives rather than a sequence of programmed instructions.

7. Perplexity sells model orchestration to enterprises (43:49)
Srinivas says Perplexity serves several tens of millions of consumers and thousands of companies, with enterprise its fastest-growing business. He gives prices of $40 a month for Enterprise Pro and $400 for Enterprise Max, says Max customers have saved more than $100 million, and says all revenue has positive gross margins even though the company is not yet profitable. He says Perplexity routes prompts across specialized models.

8. AI tools accelerate Perplexity's shipping cadence (51:17)
Srinivas calls speed Perplexity's moat and says AI coding tools let non-engineers ship code through a Slack bot. He says Computer has produced board-meeting memos, partnership decks and journalist briefings using context from earlier work. He connects these longer tasks to improvements in reasoning, tool calls and orchestration.

9. AI could help small businesses run leaner (57:29)
Srinivas says Perplexity wants to help small businesses automate marketing, payments, product updates and customer support, while acknowledging that the necessary integrations and workflows still need work. He expects job displacement but argues AI can also help people start businesses and gain more agency. He says Comet lets Computer operate browsers and that official APIs could let users authorize paid AI access to online services.

10. Open models support enterprise customization (1:07:19)
Mensch says Mistral is training its next generation of frontier models with NVIDIA to produce open models it can customize for customers. He describes Forge and Studio as tools for enterprise model specialization and agent deployment. He says 25% of Mistral's business and 25% of its researchers are in the U.S.

11. Enterprise agents need controlled access (1:11:23)
Mensch says Mistral can deploy its training and data-processing tools on customer infrastructure so data does not flow back to Mistral, then pair its engineers with domain experts to specialize models. He says synthetic data can help train smaller models, but human feedback remains necessary. For critical workflows, he calls for observable processes, sandboxes, role-based permissions and controls over which teams can access data.

12. IREN built data centers before AI demand (1:18:56)
Roberts says he and his brother started IREN with data centers for Bitcoin mining as a way to bootstrap a platform for later uses. The company is now swapping Bitcoin capacity for AI chips. He says an early 2020 Dell MOU came too soon and AI demand accelerated about two years ago. IREN has a $9.7 billion Microsoft contract, which Roberts says covers 5% of its capacity, and 4.5 gigawatts of power.

13. Power buildouts depend on local labor and renewables (1:24:40)
Roberts says IREN hires locally around its West Texas sites, has cumulatively reached $1 million in community grants, and is partnering with universities and trade colleges to build the workforce. He says IREN has used 100% renewable energy since inception, including hydro in British Columbia and wind and solar in West Texas. He cites 45 to 50 gigawatts of wind and solar in the area against 12 gigawatts of transmission capacity to Dallas and Houston, with utilities providing reliable grid power.

14. Efficiency gains can expand compute demand (1:29:27)
Roberts argues that more compute can increase usage. If ten times more capacity cut image generation to five to ten seconds, he expects people to make more images. He says NVIDIA has a major ecosystem head start while custom silicon is emerging, and that nuclear could expand U.S. compute capacity, though large projects may take a decade or longer to commission. He also discusses data-center networking and says his West Texas site has six-millisecond round-trip latency to Dallas.

The link in the reply plays each point from its second.

A TON OF THINGS HAPPENED IN THE STOCK MARKET TODAY.
Here's a full recap:

1. $AVGO Broadcom +4.00% after Bank of America, Blackstone, Citi and Morgan Stanley lined up $63B through a new SPV to buy Broadcom accelerators and networking gear and lease them to Anthropic, with deliveries from 2027. The catch is in the 8-K: Broadcom provides residual value support with peak exposure of about $43B. The SOX rose 3.6% and the Nasdaq rose 1.18%, its best day in nearly a month.

2. $AMD +5.45% after detailing its Meta partnership: Helios racks are installed and being tested at Meta, Meta will deploy a custom Instinct GPU, and AMD will invest $1B in Meta's equity offering. A supplier buying its customer's stock is becoming a habit.

3. $META fell 1.64% after upsizing that raise to a record $97.5B. The common stock portion grew to $25B priced at $625 a share, alongside $12.5B of mandatory convertible preferred and a $60B at-the-market programme from Q1 2027.

4. $ORCL Oracle +3.55% after AI World. OCI will be the first cloud outside Google to offer $GOOGL TPUs from 2027, will expand $NVDA Vera Rubin to multi-gigawatt scale, and will add $CBRS Cerebras inference and OpenAI's Jalapeño chip. Oracle also said it will use its own networking chips on some Nvidia systems. $NVDA +0.90%, $GOOGL +1.19%.

5. Neoclouds bounced hard. $NBIS Nebius +11.22% and $CRWV CoreWeave +7.94%. Nebius reportedly raised about €250M for its planned Lille data centre, days after its CEO said some financing channels had tightened. Funding access, not demand, is what this group trades on now.

6. $TSLA +4.04%, a second straight gain. Latvia became the tenth EU state to approve FSD, and Cybercabs now outnumber Model Ys in the authorised Texas robotaxi fleet.

7. After the bell, $STX Seagate beat: fiscal Q1 revenue $4.233B, adjusted EPS $7.68, and Q2 guidance of $4.8B plus or minus $100M with EPS of $9.20. Shares still fell about 6% after hours. It had closed +3.67%.

8. More chip prints, same reaction. $NXPI NXP fell about 9% after hours on Q4 revenue guidance of $3.85B versus $3.86B expected. $TER Teradyne beat with Q3 revenue of $1.306B, up 70%, and record memory test revenue on AI demand, then fell about 6%. In line is not enough at these prices.

9. $HOOD Robinhood fell almost 5% after hours. Q3 revenue was in line and average revenue per user came in at $200 versus $201.09 expected.

10. The Fed decides Wednesday. CME FedWatch shows about a 10% chance of a hike this week but better than 80% for December; the 10-year sat at 4.99% and the dollar rose for a third day. Then $MSFT and $GOOGL report after the close, $AMZN Thursday.

Broadcom guaranteed the chips, AMD bought the customer's shares, and the market called it a rally.

text:
Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, the company said on Monday, roughly a quarter of its workforce, as the tech giant seeks to cut costs while pouring money into artificial intelligence.

Staff on select teams in the United States, Canada, India and Britain at vice president level and below will be eligible, a Microsoft spokesperson said, while some groups of employees, including some working on data centres, sales and marketing, are excluded.

“The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we’re evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter,” Amy Coleman, an executive vice president and chief people officer, told employees in a memo.

It’s the second voluntary buyout offer that Microsoft has offered employees this year.

🇹🇷 Bugün piyasalarda dikkat çekici bir ayrışma yaşandı: Nasdaq %1,18 yükselişiyle günün öne çıkan endeksi olurken S&P 500 %0,60 artıda kapandı, Dow Jones ise neredeyse yatay kaldı. Korku barometresi olarak bilinen VIX %4,73 geriledi ve bu hareket, kısa vadeli bir rahatlama sinyali olarak okunabilir. Sektörler arasındaki ayrışma ise oldukça belirgindi: teknoloji %1,70 ile liderliği ele geçirdi ve yapay zeka harcamalarına olan güvenin tazelendiğine işaret etti. Anthropic'e ilişkin haberler bu iyimser tabloya katkı sağlarken, Kobeisi Letter'in vurguladığı bir nokta da kayda değer: Apple ile Nasdaq arasındaki korelasyon rekor düşük seviyelere geriledi, büyük teknoloji şirketleri artık tek bir blok gibi hareket etmiyor. Microsoft'un 60.000 çalışanına gönüllü ayrılış teklifi sunması ise yapay zeka yatırımları için alan açma stratejisinin somut bir yansıması olarak değerlendiriliyor. Makro cephede günün en kritik başlığı Fed toplantısıydı; faiz indirimi beklentisi bulunmasa da açıklamanın tonu piyasa yönü açısından belirleyici olmaya devam ediyor. Asya'dan gelen %6,71'lik Kospi yükselişi ise bölgesel iştahın güçlendiğine dair güçlü bir sinyal verdi. Jeopolitik tarafta ise Husi saldırıları enerji piyasasını hareketlendirdi; WTI ham petrol 101,50 dolara yaklaştı. Tunç Şatıroğlu'nun Fed sonrası Nasdaq stratejisi ve Kobeisi Letter'in Körfez'deki olası askeri gerginliğe yönelik uyarıları önümüzdeki günlerde yakından izlenmesi gereken başlıklar arasında yer alıyor. Yarınki seans için gözler Fed açıklamasının yansımalarında ve jeopolitik gelişmelerde olacak.

🇬🇧 Markets delivered a notable divergence today, with Nasdaq leading the charge at +1.18% while the S&P 500 closed up 0.60% and the Dow Jones barely moved from where it opened. The VIX retreated 4.73%, offering what many read as a short-term relief signal across risk assets. The sector breakdown told a clear story: technology surged 1.70%, reflecting renewed confidence in AI-related spending, partly fueled by fresh Anthropic headlines making the rounds. A point highlighted by the Kobeisi Letter added an interesting dimension — the correlation between Apple and Nasdaq has dropped to record lows, suggesting that big tech is no longer trading as a single monolithic block. Microsoft's decision to offer voluntary separation packages to 60,000 employees is being interpreted as a deliberate move to free up resources for accelerated AI investment. On the macro front, the Fed meeting dominated the agenda; while no rate cut was on the table, the tone of the statement remains the key variable markets will be parsing closely. From Asia, South Korea's KOSPI posted a striking 6.71% gain, pointing to a meaningful pickup in regional appetite. In energy markets, Houthi attacks injected fresh volatility, pushing WTI crude toward the $101.50 mark. Tunç Şatıroğlu's post-Fed Nasdaq framework and the Kobeisi Letter's warnings around potential military escalation in the Gulf are the risk threads worth tracking into the next session. Eyes remain on the Fed's aftermath and any geopolitical developments in the days ahead.

His responsibilities eventually included tracking unidentified objects in space and coordinating the recovery of crashed alien spacecraft.

2. Roswell really involved an extraterrestrial spacecraft. Becker reportedly knew a photographer who documented the 1947 crash recovery. He claimed to have seen photographs of wreckage and non-human bodies, although he did not personally witness the crash.

3. The military tracked alien spacecraft entering Earth's vicinity. According to Becker, personnel monitored deep-space radar data and tracked unidentified objects entering low Earth orbit, sometimes coordinating responses with Holloman Air Force Base.

4. American fighter jets were lost confronting UFOs. Becker alleged that U.S. military confrontations with non-human craft began during the Korean War. Aircraft losses were supposedly so serious that these intercept operations were eventually discontinued.

5. The confrontations resumed in the 1990s. Becker claimed that a massive cylindrical UFO, approximately 300 feet long, was operating dangerously close to commercial aircraft over New Mexico, prompting renewed military interception efforts.

6. A UFO apparently manipulated communications with fighter pilots. In one encounter, three military jets were reportedly ordered to return to base. All three pilots heard the instruction, but ground controllers denied issuing it. Becker suspected the unidentified craft was responsible.

7. A fighter pilot mysteriously disappeared. Following a military aircraft crash, an ejection seat, harness and deployed parachute were reportedly recovered, but the pilot was missing. Becker suspected non-human involvement.

8. There are both benevolent and malevolent non-human groups. Becker reportedly believed that some non-human intelligences abduct people for medical or scientific purposes and return them, while others take humans who never return.

9. Some government officials may be under non-human control. Becker suggested that certain people in positions of authority were being influenced or controlled by non-human intelligences. Martinez believes this could help explain the extraordinary secrecy surrounding UFOs and the confiscation of evidence.

10. The client died shortly after his story reached Congress. Martinez says he contacted Congressman Steven Schiff, who was investigating Roswell, and that Becker died unexpectedly soon afterward. Martinez also alleges that his client's file was stolen and that he experienced two suspicious incidents involving vehicles, one of which seriously injured him.

Martinez appears to be suspicious of Congressman Steven Schiff's cancer diagnosis and subsequent death, particularly because Schiff had been investigating Roswell.

In his interview with Ross Coulthart, Martinez makes several points:

Schiff had been investigating Roswell and had offered to help Martinez obtain Air Force records through FOIA requests.

Schiff subsequently developed squamous cell carcinoma, a form of skin cancer.

Martinez points out that this cancer generally has a very high five-year survival rate, approximately 99% for localized cases.

Yet Schiff's cancer progressed, and he died in March 1998.

Martinez finds the timing troubling, especially given Schiff's UFO investigation and the mysterious death of Martinez's own client.

He acknowledges that he has no direct evidence that Schiff's cancer was deliberately caused or connected to his Roswell investigation.

An important medical distinction: Schiff's cancer had spread from his ear to his face by early 1998. His disease was described as aggressive, so the survival statistics for localized squamous cell carcinoma would not necessarily apply to his case.

You can hear Martinez discuss Schiff's death at 59:35 in his Oct. 27th interview with Coulthart.

Bottom line: Martinez raises the possibility that something sinister happened to Schiff, but does not claim to possess proof that his cancer was intentionally induced.

~~~Sedge Masters/Mary Elizabeth Elliot Summary~~~

The Sedge Masters Story: Zodiac, UFO Crash Retrievals and 67 Men With Missing Memories

The Sedge Masters story is a fascinating account of a purported secret U.S. government UFO program, particularly because it includes an allegation that 67 highly trained military recovery personnel simultaneously lost 90 minutes of memory following an encounter with a large UFO.

The story appeared in three installments of UFO Magazine in 1998, written by someone using the name Greg Halifax. It was presented as fictionalized and unverified, although some researchers believe it may have been based on actual insider testimony.

Is this how Mary Elizabeth Elliot, who allegedly worked in the Legacy Program, was able to get her story out to the general public? Have her lawyer, Jeffrey Griffith, write a "fictional" story with elements of her truth in it?

~

1. The story in brief

Sedge Masters, whose full name is given as Sedgwick Masters, is a veteran CIA covert operations specialist recruited into a deeply classified UFO program called Zodiac.

He learns that:

- Zodiac allegedly oversees the retrieval and study of crashed non-human spacecraft.

- The program dates back to the late 1940s and supposedly recovered 11 spacecraft between 1947 and the 1980s.

- Some recoveries involved nonhuman occupants, including small gray beings and other reported types.

- Wright-Patterson Air Force Base allegedly houses extensive UFO records and supports recovery-related operations.

- Zodiac operates outside normal military chains of command, with extraordinary secrecy and authority.

Masters is recruited not to recover a UFO himself, but to investigate something that happened to one of Zodiac's elite retrieval teams. 

2. The 67 military personnel and their missing memories
This is arguably the most extraordinary part of the account.

67 Team members

90 Minutes missing

According to the story, the sequence unfolded as follows:

1. A UFO crashes. An elite 67-man military recovery team is dispatched to secure and retrieve a crashed craft. These men are highly experienced and trained to document their activities meticulously.

2. During the recovery operation, an enormous second craft appears above the crash site, apparently attempting to intervene.

3. A confrontation occurs. The larger UFO allegedly communicates telepathically with the recovery personnel, warning them not to take the crashed spacecraft.

4. The team experiences missing time. After the operation, every one of the 67 men is unable to account for the same approximately 90-minute interval.

5. The identical memory gaps alarm investigators. Personnel conducting debriefings at Wright-Patterson discover the consistency of the missing time across all 67 participants.

6. Masters is assigned to investigate. He participates in questioning the team commander, a colonel, alongside a psychologist. The colonel initially cannot remember the missing period either.

7. The memories suddenly return. The following day, the colonel and the other members of the team are apparently able to recall the encounter with the larger UFO.

8. The colonel attributes the memory restoration to the aliens. When asked why he can suddenly remember, the colonel says, "THEY allowed it."

9. Masters suspects the memories may have been manipulated. He wonders whether the restored recollections are genuine or whether the beings have permitted the men to recall only a carefully constructed version of what happened.

10. Further investigation is blocked. Masters proposes using hypnosis or drugs to investigate the possibility of implanted screen memories, but his superiors refuse to authorize the effort.

3. Why the memory incident is particularly interesting

The allegation isn't simply that the men forgot an encounter.

It suggests that a non-human intelligence possessed the capability to suppress and subsequently restore specific memories across an entire group of military personnel.

And the implication is even more remarkable: the beings might have controlled not only when those men remembered the incident but what they were allowed to remember.

That possibility is precisely what concerned Masters. Even after the memories returned, he couldn't be certain they reflected what actually happened.

4. The Hal Puthoff connection

This is what makes the Sedge Masters story more intriguing than an ordinary UFO tale.

On July 31, 1999, physicist Hal Puthoff sent an email to Kit Green and Kristin Zimmerman concerning the three articles.

He wrote that there was reason to believe the stories were "only slightly fictionalized versions of a source's experiences" preparing records for the archives at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base.

(That source was Mary Elizabeth Elliot, who just passed in August ~Joe)

Puthoff also asked whether Green had heard of Zodiac, supposedly the real name of the UFO control group.

That indicates that Puthoff was taking the underlying source material seriously enough to investigate.

~

And yes, he wrote a book about this. 

I'm withholding judgement for now. The first clip makes me question the judgment of Martinez. The second clip is not anything we haven't heard before in this field. Is it true? Who the hell knows?

Tel Megiddo (from Hebrew: תל מגידו; Arabic: تل المتسلم, Tell el-Muteselim) is the site of the ancient city of Megiddo (/məˈɡɪdoʊ/; Hebrew: מגידו; Greek: Μεγιδδώ), the remains of which form a tell or archaeological mound, situated in northern Israel at the western edge of the Jezreel Valley. During the Bronze Age, Megiddo was an important Canaanite city-state, and in the Iron Age, it became a royal city in the Kingdom of Israel. The site is renowned for its historical, geographical, and theological significance, especially under its Greek name Armageddon (Ἁρμαγεδών), which appears once in the Koine Greek New Testament in Revelation 16:16.

Excavations have unearthed 20 strata of ruins since the Neolithic phase, indicating a long settlement period.[1] Occupied continuously from the early Bronze Age (c. 3000 BCE) to the Persian period (c. 332 BCE), Megiddo was strategically located at the crossroads of major ancient trade routes, making it a key center for trade, politics, and military affairs. Excavations have uncovered impressive fortifications, including massive city walls and gates, as well as palaces, temples, residential buildings, and a sophisticated water system. The site is protected as Megiddo National Park and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.[2]

Assyrian period
Tiglath-Pileser III of Assyria conquered Megiddo in 732 BCE, turning it to the capital of the Neo-Assyrian Empire's province of Magiddu.[16] Hoshea (c. 732–721 BCE), the last king of the Israelite Northern Kingdom, was vassal to Tiglath-Pileser III. The site was rebuilt as an administrative center for Tiglath-Pileser III's occupation of Samaria.

Egyptian period
In 609 BCE, Megiddo was conquered by Egyptians under Necho II, during the Battle of Megiddo.

Its importance soon dwindled, and it was thought as finally abandoned around 586 BCE.[64] Since that time it would have remained uninhabited, preserving ruins pre-dating 586 BCE without settlements ever disturbing them. Archaeologist Eric Cline considers that Tel Megiddo came to an end later, around 350 BCE, during Achaemenid times.[1] Then, the town of al-Lajjun, not to be confused with the al-Lajjun archaeological site in Jordan, was built up near to the site, but without inhabiting or disturbing its remains.

Roman and Byzantine periods
During the Roman and Byzantine periods, while the site was part of the provinces of Syria Palaestina (136-390) and Palaestina Secunda (390-638), there were three settlements in the vicinity of the tell: the Jewish village of Kefar 'Othnay (Caparcotna in Latin or Kaperkotnei in Greek); Legio, the Roman military camp of the Legio VI Ferrata ('6th "Ironclad" Legion'); and later, in the 4th and 5th centuries during Byzantine rule, a polis named Maximianopolis.[65] J. Howry, processing the results of a surface reconnaissance survey in 2019 which had used LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) technology to obtain enhanced images of the ground, places Maximianopolis northwest of the tell, Legio south-southeast of it, and a village which grew next to the legion camp for which it provided services (the future Arab village of Lejjun), southwest of the tell.[66] Adams, David and Tepper (2014) write that the VIth Legion was deployed to the country sometime between 100 and 132, and was stationed there through most of the 3rd century;[65] Howry (2020) places it at Legio between 192 and 316.[66]

TPCA 2026: Taiwan’s ITRI Sees Glass Interposers as a Solution for Larger Form Factors

At TPCA 2026, Taiwan’s Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI) noted that silicon crystal growth for wafers is approaching a practical limit of around 18 inches. For larger form factors, glass could be used as an interposer material.

Square substrates are widely recognized as offering better area utilization. Interposers are typically less than 500 μm thick, with 300 × 300 mm being the most common format. Glass core substrates (GCS), by contrast, are more than 500 μm thick and are generally produced in large formats of 500 × 500 mm or greater.

As I have repeatedly noted in previous posts, ITRI is actively developing a glass interposer for TSMC.

Advantages of Glass Substrates over Conventional Organic Substrates

1. Finer wiring and support for high-frequency signals

Organic substrates reach a fine-line limit at a line width and spacing (L/S) of approximately 5/5 μm and also have relatively poor planarity. Their rough surfaces cause current diffraction and severe signal jitter at frequencies above 56 GHz.

Glass, on the other hand, has high structural rigidity and an exceptionally smooth surface. This enables fine lines below 2/2 μm and supports high-frequency applications up to 112 GHz.

2. Greater rigidity and lower thermal warpage

A 0.8 mm-thick glass substrate has more than three times the rigidity of an organic substrate of the same thickness. An organic substrate would need to be increased to 1.2 mm in thickness to achieve comparable rigidity.

Even at that thickness, however, the organic substrate experiences three times more thermal warpage than a glass substrate of the same thickness.

3. Excellent high-frequency electrical performance

Glass maintains losses below 0.7 dB even at 120 GHz. Through-glass via (TGV) loss is reduced by 56% at the same thickness and by 70% at equivalent rigidity.

4. Controllable warpage and tunable thermal expansion

Glass substrates offer controllable warpage and a tunable coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE). As a silicon-based material, glass inherently has a CTE close to that of silicon, and its properties can be fine-tuned through the addition of dopants.

Conventional organic carriers have a CTE approximately five times higher than that of glass.

Duster Hybrid - Crisp Analysis 

✅ Returned 19 kmpl after 80 km of use in Chennai traffic and highway usage

✅ Engine note is excellent, is eager to perform, feels outright and powerful 

✅ Hybrid system works dynamically & very fast, it remains eager to charge the battery and on low speeds that process feels aggressive with a buzz on your pedal & steering

✅ Upshifting feels super smooth but downshifting is slightly noticeable 

✅ The way tech works in real time, you feel like this is dirt cheap under 20L with 4-cyl, 1800 cc, 160 ps, 208 nm torque and fuel efficiency on offer.

✅ E-Save mode is good to have to manually charge your 1.4 kWh battery by keeping engine involved most of the time

✅ Precise steering, good feedback, excellent suspension with FDD and overall control. One of the best in segment to drive and with hybrid, no compromise on power in any way. Turning radius felt less too and it was easy to use in traffic.

✅ On low speeds, EV mode helps in good acceleration but regen engage early that you like. Honda City did well there in regen & overall smoothness that we drove a few months back. Duster returned 19 kmpl but it can easily return 20+ in mild traffic with AC because I took a lot of videos/shots with a static car and AC on. 

✅ All variants are extremely VFM, I don’t think brand is looking to make any profits initially.

✅ Bootspace isn’t compromised and 7 yr of extended warranty is good to have without paying extra. You just need to stick with service centre for your oil service to fulfil this condition. 

✅ Physical buttons, One touch up down windows with anti pinch are highly appreciated. 

⚠️ Cabin feels slightly tighter as compared to other cars in this segment like Sierra, Seltos & Creta. Roof is slightly low. Glass area feels average.

⚠️ Downshifting was slightly noticeable and that regen ‘buzz’ on the pedal might irritate some drivers.

⚠️ Renault’s thin dealership & service network and long term ownership cost for this tech after 7 yr is unknown. Warranty on battery is 8 yr

Verdict - 9 out of 10 as a package. Perfect for four as a family car with running above 1000 km looking for fuel efficiency, looks, performance, dynamics and comfort.

text:
Did His Passion Fail Him, or Was It Our Company's Loss?
#LJBStories

Some time back, we recruited a young man into our tech team at @lwegatech.

We went through the interviews, and he appeared eager, enthusiastic, ready to learn and, most importantly, passionate about #technology.

And you know, almost every developer I've interviewed these days introduces themselves as a Full-Stack Developer.......Hahahaha! 😂

Anyway, after the interview, we offered him a position primarily focused on front-end and website development.

As you may know, LWEGATECH provides website development, website maintenance, software development and other technology services.

We clearly explained that his primary responsibility would be in the web department, although other technical assignments could come his way.

He accepted the offer.

The first month? Everything was merry! 😂

Then came the stage where enthusiasm had to translate into results.

You know that moment when you're no longer just learning from colleagues, but you're expected to take ownership of assignments, solve problems independently and deliver a complete project?

Well, that's when the cracks started appearing.

The young man began expressing his frustrations to colleagues.

Apparently, he hadn't signed up to be a web developer!

He considered himself a backend developer and preferred working on software and application development rather than websites.

Now, we're not a very big team, so you can imagine how quickly that information reached my desk. 😂

I called him in for a quick one-on-one conversation.
After listening to him, he finally said:
"Sir, my passion is backend development. I don't like web development."

I asked him:
"But during your interview, you told us you're a full-stack developer. We also explained the responsibilities of this position, and you accepted them. What changed along the way?"

Silence!

Of course, you can imagine what happened next.

But long after that conversation, I found myself asking a question.

Did his passion fail him, or was this our company's loss?

Because here's the interesting part.

If this young man had told us during the interview that he was passionate about backend development and had no interest in front-end or website development, we probably wouldn't have offered him that particular position.

Not because backend development is less important, but because that wasn't the position we were recruiting for.

We hired based on the skills he presented, the responsibilities we explained and the agreement we reached.

So when someone accepts a role and later declares that their passion lies elsewhere, where does that leave the employer?

And this brings me to something I've been thinking about.

Are we sometimes too quick to introduce ourselves using professional titles and industry jargon without fully appreciating what those titles mean or the responsibilities they carry?

There's absolutely nothing wrong with being passionate about backend development.

In fact, specialisation is a wonderful thing.

But there's a difference between saying "I'm a full-stack developer who prefers backend work" and accepting a front-end position only to later say "I don't do front-end development."

My friends, passion is important.

But so are honesty, clarity and understanding what you're committing yourself to.

Sometimes being honest about what you cannot or do not want to do can save both you and your prospective employer a great deal of trouble.

Now, back to my question:
Did his passion fail him, or did the company lose out?

What would you have done differently?

Have a wonderful Wednesday, friends! 😊

Some takeaways from the Lakers- trailblazers game:

- first loss of the season, so this is what it feels like to be sad again. We couldn't go 82-0 anyways so we have to move on. Next game is a rematch against our lil bros, the clippers. We can bounce back with a win. 

- Luka Dončić had another fantastic game with 41 points, making 6 three-pointers. He slowed down in the fourth quarter, attempting just three field goals. It was a combination of Portland's extremely good point-of-attack defense and some fatigue (?) Dončić had just 2 turnovers while dishing out 9 assists. 

- Austin Reaves scored 26 points while dishing out 7 assists and 0 turnovers. AR made four threes, he's shooting 57% from behind-the-arc. He's extremely confident in his shot right now. 

-Ziaire Williams. What a signing. We need to start figuring out how much of the mle we will offer him. Continues to be a sniper from the corner, making two corner threes tonight.

- Sandro Mamukelashvili is so good as power forward. We just need to get a springy back up center to make all the pieces fit perfectly. 

-Kevon Looney shouldn't be playing but JJ Redick is still not interested in using Vando as a backup big. What's the worst that can happen? Vanderbilt averaged 9.3 rebounds per 36 last season. He shot 37.5 percent-just below league average of 38-on corner threes just two seasons ago. He's at least worth a shot. 

-Longterm, a trade needs to happen to fix the back up 5 problem. It's a huge hole that's putting stress on the team. This was a clean game turnover wise, we shot the ball well, 56% from the field and 40% from three and had more stocks than Portland (10 to 7). So what happened? They outrebounded us and we committed silly fouls whenever we started building a lead and momentum. 

- All in all, I'll chalk up today's loss to outrebounding and fatigue. We have been using 9-man rotations essentially against 10-man rotations. One year ago in Kuala Lumpur, India and the US signed a 10-year defence framework.

Today in Cebu, @rajnathsingh and @SecWar Pete Hegseth met to mark its first anniversary, on the sidelines of the ADMM-Plus meeting of ASEAN defence ministers.

What they reviewed:
1. Military technology
2. Information sharing
3. Co-production, which means making weapons together, in India

That is the official line. Now the harder part.

The framework names co-production areas like surveillance, undersea tracking, air combat and munitions. It also wants India to become a repair and maintenance hub for the region.

But the deal that matters most is still not signed. The GE F414 jet engine, to be made with HAL for the Tejas Mk2, was announced in June 2023. HAL says the technical talks are done. It is still waiting for GE's price offer.

The IAF has 29 fighter squadrons against 42 sanctioned. Every month of delay hurts.

My read as a realist: Washington wants India as a weight against China in the Indo-Pacific. India wants technology, not just purchase orders. Both get what they want only if the engine deal closes.

Hegseth also met the defence ministers of Japan, Australia and South Korea here. Those three are US allies. India is a partner, not an ally, and talks to everyone.

My bet: GE's price offer reaches HAL by December, but the final F414 contract slips to mid-2027.

Watch for Rajnath Singh's speech to ADMM-Plus on Thursday.

text:
🇺🇸 Miami 2027: The New Geography of Power

Miami has always reinvented itself. Once a gateway to Latin America, it is now emerging as a crossroads where American diplomacy, global capital and transnational political networks intersect, bringing seemingly unrelated actors and agendas into the same orbit. Its latest transformation may be less about geography than about influence.

The pattern is becoming increasingly visible. Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have been involved in high-level discussions with Russian, Ukrainian, European and Middle Eastern officials, with South Florida serving as a venue for negotiations over Ukraine and Gaza. This approach relies heavily on personal relationships and trusted intermediaries, with political negotiations often linked to economic incentives.

The geography helps explain Miami’s appeal. The city combines Latin American diaspora communities, conservative political networks, deep financial infrastructure and easy access to Washington. International negotiations and domestic political movements can operate side by side — and sometimes intersect.

The Brazilian dimension adds another layer. Following his defeat to Lula, Flávio Bolsonaro arrived in the United States after visas were confirmed for him and his family. In South Florida, the Bolsonaro family can draw on an established Brazilian diaspora, political allies and business networks cultivated over the years by their father, Jair Bolsonaro. These connections offer a platform for continued political visibility, transnational mobilisation and engagement with the US administration.

Yet Miami’s significance extends well beyond Latin America. Renewed Arab interest in American diplomacy, investment and regional security adds another dimension, as Gulf capital and Middle Eastern diplomatic initiatives intersect with broader discussions about reconstruction, energy infrastructure and regional stability. These parallel networks may converge in Miami without forming part of a single geopolitical project. The question is whether proximity and personal connections will translate into lasting cooperation.

That distinction matters. Personal diplomacy can open doors, but it can also blur the boundaries between public authority, private interests and political influence. Lasting agreements still require institutions, enforceable commitments and accountability.

Three tests will determine whether Miami’s influence endures: whether talks translate into lasting agreements, whether access to power survives the ebb and flow of personal relationships and political favour, and whether democratic oversight can keep pace with increasingly informal diplomacy.

Miami’s power lies in its connections, not its formal authority. A switchboard is not a capital: it routes power without owning it. And in a city defined by reinvention, the next chapter will depend on whether those connections can turn access into lasting influence.

The message is clear: planners can no longer assume the next major war will stay overseas. 

That raises urgent questions about civilian preparedness. America’s reliance on foreign-made electrical equipment has fueled concerns about power-grid vulnerabilities. Officials have investigated Chinese-made transformers and undocumented communications devices in power inverters, although a later Energy Department investigation found no evidence those devices were malicious. 

Meanwhile, Britain’s defense secretary is urging households to keep emergency supplies for natural disasters and disruptions involving terrorists or hostile states. With Middle East tensions rising, what happens if electricity, communications, and supply chains fail together?

None of this proves an imminent global war or a secret plan. Preparing for catastrophe does not mean catastrophe is coming. But if military bases are planning to keep operating while surrounding infrastructure fails, Americans deserve to know the civilian plan.
