But on a serious note, I believe 30% is a reasonable starting point to consider when negotiating an advance payment, but it is NOT a universal rule for every project.

The suitable percentage depends on the contract terms, the cost of mobilisation, the materials required, the project duration, the payment structure and the risks involved.

Let’s use this same project as an example.

For a 1.5 billion project:

10% advance = 150 million
20% advance = 300 million
30% advance = 450 million

The 200 million offered is approximately 13.3% of the project value.

Now, is that too small? It depends on what the contractor needs to spend before receiving the next payment.

For a project that requires expensive machinery, imported equipment, bulk material purchases and significant mobilisation costs, 200 million might not be enough.

However, if the contractor doesn’t need much money upfront and the client has a reliable payment structure based on milestones, a lower advance could work perfectly well.

For example, imagine a contractor needs 350 million to purchase equipment and materials before work can progress. An advance of 200 million would leave a funding gap of 150 million. That gap must be covered somehow, either through the contractor’s own funds, agreed supplier credit or another financing arrangement.

That is why contractors should not negotiate advance payments based on percentages alone. They should calculate the actual cash required to get the project moving.

My advice to contractors: Before accepting a major project, prepare a cash-flow forecast, estimate your mobilisation costs, identify your initial material requirements and understand when subsequent payments will arrive. Then negotiate an advance that matches the project’s actual funding needs.

My advice to clients: Don’t choose an advance percentage arbitrarily. Ask the contractor to justify the amount with a cost breakdown, and agree on appropriate safeguards, documentation and recovery terms.

Remember, 30% is a negotiation benchmark some contractors may consider, not a mandatory industry standard or a percentage that automatically suits every contract. The right figure is the one that supports project execution while keeping both parties financially protected.

Now, let me ask my fellow construction professionals:

For a 1.5 billion rice mill project, would you accept 200 million upfront, negotiate for 30%, or calculate the advance based on actual mobilisation costs?

Let’s hear your reasons.

text:
Other Princes Searched for Rare Delicacies. He Won the Throne with Rice.

Vietnamese legend tells of a king who asked his sons to prepare offerings for their ancestors. The one whose offering pleased him would inherit the throne.

The other princes searched the mountains and seas for precious foods.

Lang Liêu, the poorest among them, turned to familiar ingredients: sticky rice, mung beans and pork.

He prepared two kinds of rice cakes.

One was square, wrapped in leaves, with a filling of mung beans and pork. It represented the earth.

The other was round, made from pounded sticky rice. It represented the sky.

The king chose Lang Liêu as his successor.

The square cake was bánh chưng. Its round companion was bánh giầy.

This is a legend associated with the sixth Hùng King, not a documented account of how the foods were invented. But the tradition it explains remains alive.

During Tết, Vietnam’s Lunar New Year, families still prepare bánh chưng and offer it to their ancestors. Leaves are folded, rice and fillings packed inside, and the cakes boiled for hours.

A royal succession story survives in something people can unwrap, share and eat.

For those who grew up with bánh chưng, what comes back first: its taste, or the people who made it with you?

text:
$DASH — Dash ⚡

Bitcoin proved that digital money could exist.

Dash tried to make it practical for everyday payments.

Instant settlement.
Low transaction fees.
Optional privacy.
Decentralized governance.

More than a decade later, DASH is still operating.

But the token trades roughly 97% below its historical peak.

Here's the question.

Is Dash a forgotten payment network with genuine utility, or has the market moved on to stablecoins and newer blockchains?
⠀
01 | WHAT IS DASH?

Dash is a cryptocurrency launched in 2014, originally designed for fast, inexpensive digital payments.

Its infrastructure includes:

• InstantSend — Fast payment confirmation
• ChainLocks — Protection against chain reorganizations
• CoinJoin — Optional transaction privacy
• Masternodes — Network services and governance
• Dash Platform — Application and data infrastructure
• DASH — Native payment and network asset

Unlike many newer tokens, DASH isn't primarily a governance claim on a DeFi application.

It is the currency powering its own blockchain.

That creates direct utility.

But utility alone doesn't guarantee growing demand.
⠀
02 | WHERE DOES DEMAND COME FROM?

Three major sources:

• Payments and transfers
• Masternode collateral
• Network services and ecosystem activity

DASH is required for transactions.

Traditional masternodes require 1,000 DASH in collateral, while Evolution masternodes require more.

That creates a meaningful reason to hold tokens.

But there's a limitation.

A payment token can circulate quickly without investors needing to hold it for long periods.

High transaction activity doesn't automatically mean sustained buying pressure.

Velocity matters.
⠀
03 | THE BIG NARRATIVE 🔥

Three potential catalysts:

• Renewed demand for payment cryptocurrencies
• Expansion of Dash Evolution
• Growing interest in financial privacy

Bitcoin increasingly serves as a store-of-value asset.

Stablecoins dominate dollar-denominated crypto payments.

Dash occupies a different position.

A decentralized payment network with optional privacy and built-in governance.

The opportunity?

Demand returns for cryptocurrencies designed to function as money.

The risk?

Users prefer stablecoins because they don't want payment volatility.

Dash must compete on actual usefulness, not nostalgia.
⠀
04 | THE COMPETITIVE ADVANTAGE

Dash has several established strengths.

• More than a decade of operation
• Fast transaction confirmation
• Low network fees
• Masternode infrastructure
• Decentralized treasury funding
• Optional privacy functionality

Its governance model is particularly distinctive.

Part of newly issued DASH funds community-approved development and ecosystem proposals.

But competition is intense.

$LTC offers established payment infrastructure.

$XMR has stronger privacy-focused positioning.

Stablecoins offer predictable dollar value.

Dash needs to demonstrate why users should choose DASH over these alternatives.
⠀
05 | THE NUMBERS 📊

October 28, 2026 market snapshot:

• Price: ~$55
• Market cap: ~$708M
• Maximum-supply FDV: ~$1.04B
• Circulating supply: ~12.88M DASH
• Maximum potential supply: ~18.92M DASH
• Circulating percentage: ~68%
• 24H trading volume: ~$116M
• Historical ATH: ~$1,642
• Decline from ATH: ~96.7%

Recent DeFiLlama chain tracking also showed:

• Daily active addresses: ~34K
• Daily transactions: ~11K
• Daily chain fees: ~$23
• Tracked DeFi TVL: ~$96K

These metrics require context.

Dash is primarily a payments network, not a DeFi-first blockchain.

Low DeFi TVL doesn't mean the payment network has no users.

But the economic challenge is obvious.

Network fee generation remains extremely small relative to market capitalization.
⠀
06 | THE TOKENOMICS TRAP

Dash has no conventional venture-capital token allocation waiting to unlock.

Its supply is created through block rewards.

Current block-subsidy allocation:

• 20% — Miners
• 60% — Masternode rewards
• 20% — Decentralized governance budget

The maximum eventual supply is approximately 18.92M DASH, depending on treasury allocations.

But here's the trap.

A limited supply doesn't mean zero inflation.

New DASH continues entering circulation.

And masternode rewards aren't automatically profits generated by paying customers.

Much of the reward system is funded through newly issued coins.

A scarcity narrative needs real demand behind it.
⠀
07 | THE NEXT BIG UNLOCK

Dash doesn't have a conventional monthly insider unlock calendar.

There is no major VC vesting cliff comparable to newer altcoins.

Instead, supply expands through ongoing block rewards.

Dash reduces its block subsidy by approximately 7.14% every 210,240 blocks, roughly once a year.

This gradually slows issuance.

But future supply still matters.

And masternode collateral isn't permanently removed from circulation.

Operators can eventually release and sell their holdings.

The key risk is continuous issuance and changing holder demand.

Not a single scheduled insider unlock.
⠀
08 | THE VALUE CAPTURE PROBLEM 👀

This is the central investment debate.

Dash has a direct economic relationship between network usage and DASH.

Users pay transaction fees in the native asset.

Masternodes lock DASH as collateral.

But consider the distinction:

• Payment volume — Value transferred
• Transaction fees — Paid by network users
• Block rewards — Newly issued DASH
• Masternode rewards — Compensation for network services
• Holder earnings — Not automatic dividends

The network's low fees are excellent for payments.

But they generate limited direct economic revenue.

Masternode yields also need to be evaluated against token inflation and price risk.

A high nominal reward doesn't necessarily create real investment returns.

Dash needs stronger organic payment demand to support its long-term valuation.
⠀
09 | FINAL VERDICT 🎯

Dash has genuine strengths.

Established infrastructure.

Fast payments.

A limited supply.

Decentralized governance.

And a long operating history.

But it faces a difficult competitive reality.

Stablecoins dominate many practical crypto-payment use cases.

And privacy-focused cryptocurrencies compete for users seeking financial confidentiality.

The bullish case?

Dash Evolution expands functionality, payment adoption strengthens, and reduced issuance supports a healthier supply-demand balance.

The bearish case?

The network remains technically functional but fails to attract enough new users and capital.

Meanwhile, competing payment systems continue gaining market share.

🔥 DASH doesn't need to prove that it can survive.

It has already survived multiple market cycles.

It needs to prove that people still want to use it.

Survival is impressive.

Adoption is what determines the next chapter.

Save this before the next payment-coin rotation.

$DASH  vs $LTC vs $XMR — which has the strongest long-term use case?

Is DASH an overlooked survivor, or is its discount justified by changing market demand?

Drop your pick below. 👇

text:
The History of the Music Man StingRay Guitar, 1976-2026

Music Man emerged in the early 1970s through Tom Walker and Forrest White, both associated with Fender. Leo Fender joined the company in 1975, helping develop a new generation of electric instruments. Introduced in 1976, the StingRay guitar represented one of his most ambitious departures from traditional Fender designs.

1976-1982 - StingRay I and II

The original StingRay featured a solid ash body, bolt-on maple neck, 25.5” scale, two humbucking pickups and active electronics. Unlike conventional passive guitar circuits, its battery-powered preamplifier provided bass and treble equalization, expanding the instrument’s frequency-shaping capabilities.

The StingRay I featured a 12” fingerboard radius and 22 jumbo frets. The StingRay II offered a 7.5” radius and 22 standard frets. Both employed four-position pickup switching and a separate bright switch.

The pickups used Alnico magnets and conventional electromagnetic coils feeding the active preamplifier. This distinction is important: the original StingRay was an active-electronics guitar, not simply a guitar fitted with unusually powerful pickups.

Despite its advanced circuitry, the StingRay struggled commercially. Leo Fender departed Music Man in 1980, and guitar production ended around 1982.

1984-2015 - The Ernie Ball Era

Ernie Ball acquired Music Man in 1984. While the StingRay bass became a cornerstone of the company, the guitar remained discontinued for more than three decades.

2016 - StingRay Returns

Ernie Ball Music Man revived the StingRay with a redesigned African mahogany body, five-bolt maple neck, 25.5” scale, 22 stainless steel frets, dual passive humbuckers, five-way switching and modern tremolo.

Unlike the original, the revived StingRay emphasized passive electronics and contemporary construction rather than active equalization.

2018 - StingRay RS

The RS introduced roasted maple neck construction, revised appointments and expanded finishes. Its passive humbuckers, stainless steel frets and modern tremolo continued the 2016 design philosophy. Body woods varied across production.

2022 - StingRay HT

The HT introduced a heat-treated bridge humbucker, ceramic-magnet neck humbucker and onboard boost circuit. Its active electronics offered up to 20 dB of adjustable boost, while the guitar incorporated an alder body, roasted maple neck and Tune-o-matic-style bridge.

Legacy

The StingRay’s evolution illustrates two distinct approaches to electric guitar engineering: Leo Fender’s pioneering active equalization in 1976 and Ernie Ball Music Man’s modern combination of passive pickups, specialized magnets and selective active circuitry.

The original StingRay remains an important, relatively uncommon chapter in Leo Fender’s career, while its modern descendants preserve the name through substantially redesigned instruments.

EAAA INDIA ALTERNATIVES IPO: LAST DAY TODAY (28 Oct)

📌 THE OFFER

Price band: ₹1,585–1,665
Issue size: ₹1,200 crore
Fresh issue: ₹0
OFS: ₹1,200 crore (100%)
Lot size: 9 shares
Minimum investment: ₹14,985 at ₹1,665
Retail quota: at least 35% (QIBs up to 50%, NIIs at least 15%)

Dates:
Opened: 26 October
Closes: TODAY, 28 October (accept the UPI mandate by 5 PM)
Expected allotment: 29 October
Tentative listing: 2 November on BSE and NSE
Registrar: MUFG Intime India

🏦 WHAT DOES EAAA DO?

It is the alternative investment arm of the Edelweiss group. It was earlier called Edelweiss Alternative Asset Advisors.

It manages ₹95,345 crore of client money in two main businesses:

Real Assets: infrastructure and commercial real estate through 10 funds, including 2 InvITs
Private Credit: lending to companies outside the banking system (performing credit, special situations, real estate credit) through 16 funds
Fees are earned on ₹48,623 crore of fee-paying AUM, about half the total.

It has 11,009 client relationships. 49% of AUM comes from institutions and 34% from foreign clients. Offices: Mumbai, Delhi, GIFT City and Singapore.

📊 FY26 PERFORMANCE

Total income: ₹964 crore, up 22.5%
Management fees: ₹579 crore, up 20.8%
Performance fees: ₹290 crore, up 52.3%
PAT: ₹265 crore, up only 15.4%
PAT margin: 27.5%, down from 30.0% in FY24
Q1 FY27: total income ₹336 crore (up 58.8%) and PAT ₹81 crore (up 45%). That PAT includes ₹54 crore of mark-to-market gains on its own fund investments.

✅ WHAT WORKS IN ITS FAVOUR

India's first listed pure-play alternatives manager, in a fast-growing sector

Sticky clients: 77% of AUM comes from repeat clients
Fee-paying AUM grew 21% a year, from ₹30,398 crore in FY24 to ₹44,710 crore in FY26

Real Assets fee-paying AUM grew 46% in one year
ROE of about 26%

Low debt: borrowings of ₹399 crore, or ₹0.34 for every ₹1 of net worth

Mutual funds took 65% of the anchor book

⚠️ WHAT HOLDS ME BACK

100% OFS. The full ₹1,200 crore goes to Edelweiss Securities and the company gets nothing.

The promoter's average cost is ₹54.45 per share, so it is exiting at about 30 times its cost. Group companies bought shares at ₹925 in Sept 2025, and the IPO price is 1.8 times that just 13 months later.

Much of the profit is still on paper. Performance fees are booked as unrealised gains. After the linked employee bonuses, they came to ₹129 crore, about half of FY26 PBT. Of the ₹685 crore booked since FY24, ₹287 crore has not been received in cash.

Cash lags profit. From FY24 to Q1 FY27, PAT was ₹751 crore but operating cash flow was only ₹232 crore. 

Operating cash flow was negative in FY24 and FY25.
High costs: the cost-to-income ratio is 64%, against 20–38% for listed AMCs.

SEBI history:

SEBI returned the first DRHP in March 2025 over "reclassification between revenue lines"

After an inspection, SEBI issued administrative warnings in July 2026 for not following investment processes and investor disclosure rules

A settlement application is pending

Leadership churn: the MD & CEO quit in Sept 2025, the head of real estate credit in April 2026 and a co-CEO in June 2026.

The current CEO was paid ₹39.75 crore in FY26, about 15% of PAT.

A ₹206 crore pre-IPO dividend (₹32 per share) went almost entirely to the promoter.

Edelweiss group baggage: RBI orders against ECL Finance and Edelweiss ARC in 2024 (since lifted), a police FIR that names the company, and a ₹34 crore tax demand.

💰 VALUATION

At ₹1,665, the market cap is about ₹10,765 crore. That is 40.4× FY26 EPS of ₹41.26, against 39.89× for the RHP's peer group. Price to book is 9.4×.

360 ONE trades at 35.7× and Nuvama at 31×. AMCs trade at 28–46×, but they run PAT margins above 50%.

Remove the performance fees that are still on paper and you are paying about 66× core earnings.

My fair value range: ₹1,210–1,610 (30–40× FY26 diluted EPS). My base case is ₹1,413 (35×), about 15% below the IPO price. There is no margin of safety.

🏛️ ANCHOR BOOK

₹360 crore was allocated across 26 anchor allocations at ₹1,665, the top of the band. That is 30% of the issue.

SBI Midcap Fund: ₹38 crore
ICICI Pru Smallcap Fund: ₹38 crore
HDFC MF: ₹38 crore across 2 schemes
Nippon India MF: ₹38 crore across 2 schemes
Kotak MF: ₹20.5 crore across 2 schemes
Carnelian Bharat Amritkaal Fund: ₹20.5 crore
Schroders: ₹18.4 crore across 2 funds
Norway's Government Pension Fund Global: ₹10 crore
Mutual funds took 65.42% of the book, across 10 AMCs and 13 schemes. No insurer or pension fund bid. 

Goldman Sachs and BNP came in through ODIs, ₹5 crore each.

Nuvama is a lead manager, and its EDGE fund took ₹5 crore. 360 ONE, a listed competitor, took ₹11 crore.

Lock-in: 50% for 30 days (about 28 Nov) and 50% for 90 days.

📊 SUBSCRIPTION (Day 3)
QIB: 1.01×
NII: 1.30×
Retail: 0.17× 🚨
Total: 0.65×

The issue is still not fully covered on the last day. Retail has bid for less than a fifth of its quota.

📈 GMP

GMP was ₹10 (0.6%) as of 27 Oct, 4 PM, pointing to a listing near ₹1,675. It peaked at ₹121 (7.27%) on 23 Oct, so it fell more than 90% in four days.

📝 MY VIEW

I am not applying. Weak demand on the last day and an almost flat GMP confirm my view: the valuation leaves no room for upside, either at listing or over the long term.

Not SEBI registered. Educational purposes only. Do your own research. GMP is unofficial and listing gains are not assured.
